whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence: "It was the kind of challenge that would set any art curator's mind into motion." What follows — "finding that elusive thread that could link artists as disparate as..." — is not a sentence; it names what the challenge actually was. A colon is the mark that lets a complete sentence introduce an explanation or specification like that, so "motion: finding" is the only version that punctuates the two parts correctly.

whyWrong.A: Puts the colon after "finding" instead of before it, so the colon interrupts "finding" from its own object, "that elusive thread" — a colon can never separate a verb from what it acts on.
whyWrong.B: A period demands a complete sentence on each side, and "Finding that elusive thread that could link artists..." has no main verb; it is a fragment.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but the material after the blank is a participial phrase, not a clause that could stand alone.

commonMistakes: Assuming any of the four marks will do because the phrase after the blank is long; length has nothing to do with it — only whether each side can stand alone.
tips: Test the words after the blank on their own: if they cannot be a sentence, a period and a semicolon are both out, which usually leaves the colon.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "Currently," which fixes the time frame as right now, and describing a species' present-day range calls for the simple present. "Includes" is the only choice in that tense, and it agrees with the singular subject "the frog's range."

whyWrong.A: The present perfect "has included" describes something that began earlier and continues, which conflicts with "Currently" pointing at the present moment alone.
whyWrong.B: The future perfect "will have included" places the action before some later point in the future — nothing in the text sets up a future reference point.
whyWrong.D: The simple past "included" says the range was that way at some finished earlier time, contradicting "Currently."

tips: When a sentence hands you a time marker like "Currently," "In 1902," or "By next year," match the verb to that marker before you look at anything else.

whyCorrect: Look at what comes after the comma: "both the Orden Hijos de América (1921) and the Partido Nacional de La Raza Unida (1970) contributed to the history of US civil rights" is a complete sentence with its own subject and verb. "The 20th century saw the founding of many Latino advocacy groups" is also a complete sentence. Two complete sentences cannot be joined by a comma, so the blank has to end the first one with a period. That leaves "Established to protect and advance the rights of Latino Americans" as an opening participial phrase modifying the two organizations that follow it.

whyWrong.A: "and established" makes "the 20th century" the thing that established something, and it still leaves a comma splice before "both the Orden..."
whyWrong.B: Attaching "established to protect..." to "groups" keeps the first half a complete sentence, so the comma before "both the Orden..." joins two independent clauses — a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: Same splice as B; adding a comma after "groups" changes only how the modifier is set off, not the illegal comma joining the two sentences.

commonMistakes: Choosing based on how the modifier sounds next to "groups" without checking that the second half of the sentence is independent.

whyCorrect: The end of the text — "the method emphasizes learning from skilled musicians... and teaches students as young as three..." — is a full sentence with its own subject, "the method." So the words before it must be a separate sentence, and the only complete one available is "The pedagogy of the Suzuki method is rooted in several central tenets." A period at the blank does that, and "Developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, who sought to parallel the linguistic learning environment," then works as an opening modifier describing the method.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "tenets developed by... Suzuki, who sought to parallel the linguistic learning environment, the method emphasizes..." runs one complete sentence straight into another.
whyWrong.B: A comma after "tenets" still leaves two independent clauses joined only by commas — a splice, not a fix.
whyWrong.D: "tenets that, developed by..." starts a relative clause with "that" and then never gives it a verb, so the clause is left dangling.

tips: Find the sentence's real main verb first — here it is "emphasizes" — then check whether the words before it can stand alone.

whyCorrect: "The Serna v. Portales Schools court decision in 1974, which affirmed the rights of Latino students, is another such event" is a complete sentence, so the words before it must end with a period, not a comma. Putting "for one" at the end of the first sentence also keeps it attached to the right thing: El Teatro Campesino is the "one" example, and the Serna decision is then "another."

whyWrong.A: Joins two complete sentences with only a comma after "for one" — a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: Same comma splice, and it also drops the comma that should set off "for one" as an interrupter.
whyWrong.D: Grammatically it ends the sentence, but it moves "For one" onto the Serna decision, which the same sentence calls "another such event" — you cannot introduce something as both the first example and an additional one.

commonMistakes: Treating this as a pure punctuation question and stopping once you find an option that ends the first sentence; here you also have to see which side "for one" belongs on.

whyCorrect: "The gaseous compounds" on its own does not tell you which compounds, so the names "thymol and methane" are essential information and take no commas around them. Once you drop the commas, nothing separates the subject "the gaseous compounds thymol and methane" from its verb "have," which is exactly what Standard English requires.

whyWrong.A: Opens a nonessential element with a comma after "compounds" but never closes it before "have," leaving the punctuation unpaired.
whyWrong.B: Pairs the commas correctly but marks the names as nonessential, which would mean the sentence already identifies the compounds without them — it does not.
whyWrong.D: Places a single comma between the complete subject and the verb "have," which is never allowed.

tips: Ask whether the noun phrase before the names already points to something specific; if it does not, the names are essential and get no commas.

whyCorrect: The two sentences are events in sequence: Gomez won a competition in 2014, and then in 2017 he created a show. The transition only needs to mark that the second event came after the first, which is what "Later" does.

whyWrong.A: "Instead" signals that the second thing replaced the first, but creating the show did not take the place of winning the competition.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would make the show an instance of winning a storytelling competition, and it is not — it is a separate thing he founded.
whyWrong.D: "In other words" introduces a restatement of the same idea, but the second sentence gives new information rather than rephrasing the first.

tips: When both sentences carry dates, check whether the relationship is just chronological before reaching for a fancier transition.

whyCorrect: The clause before the semicolon says what Chaucer did not write in, and the clause after it supplies the correct alternative. That negation-then-correction pattern calls for "rather," which means "instead, the truth is this."

whyWrong.B: "Finally" marks the last item in a sequence, but nothing here is being listed in order.
whyWrong.C: "As a result" claims the second clause is caused by the first; writing Middle English is not an effect of not writing Modern English, it is the same fact stated positively.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" signals a parallel between two like things, but the two clauses contrast a denial with a correction.

tips: A negative statement followed by the accurate version almost always takes "rather" or "instead."

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank gives one reason Honeoye suits the role of state soil — it is abundant. The sentence after gives a second, separate reason — it supports agriculture. Adding a reason on top of a reason calls for an additive transition, which is "Moreover."

whyWrong.A: "At that time" points back to a specific moment already named, and the passage never establishes one.
whyWrong.B: "Alternatively" offers a competing option, but the agricultural role does not replace or compete with the abundance point.
whyWrong.C: "Conversely" signals a reversal, yet both sentences argue the same way — that Honeoye is a fitting state soil.

commonMistakes: Picking a contrast word because the second sentence introduces something new; new is not the same as opposed.

whyCorrect: The goal is to state one element's relative abundance on Earth, so the sentence has to name an element, name Earth, and give the actual figure. Only the potassium sentence does all three by reporting its mass fraction as a percentage on Earth. The other choices describe how abundance can be measured, or compare two elements, without ever stating a value.

whyWrong.A: Lists the three ways abundance can be expressed; it never gives any element's abundance on Earth.
whyWrong.C: Says potassium's abundance can be expressed three ways but withholds the number, so nothing is specified.
whyWrong.D: Compares two elements rather than specifying an abundance, and the comparison contradicts the notes — potassium's 0.016% is far smaller than calcium's 1.71%.

tips: Turn the stated goal into a checklist of the pieces the sentence must contain, then eliminate anything missing a piece.

whyCorrect: The goal is a similarity, so the sentence has to mention both artifacts and state something they share. Only this choice names the spoon and the purse together and points to what is true of each — both sit in the Hina Hanta archive and both are Choctaw cultural artifacts.

whyWrong.A: Mentions only the spoon, so there is no second item to be similar to.
whyWrong.C: Uses the 1949 date to draw a distinction about dates rather than a shared trait, and the spoon appears only by implication.
whyWrong.D: Frames the two artifacts as different in age, which is a contrast, the opposite of what the goal asks for.

tips: For a "similarity" goal, require both subjects in the sentence and a shared property — a date comparison is a contrast even when both items appear.

whyCorrect: A similarity sentence needs both positions plus a trait they hold in common. The notes say first position and demi-seconde position are each a position for the dancer's arms, and that is the one thing the notes state about both. This choice names both and gives exactly that shared feature.

whyWrong.B: Misstates the notes: first position belongs to the Vaganova method, not the Royal Academy of Dance.
whyWrong.C: Names both positions but its "in contrast to" wording sets them against each other, emphasizing the difference in arm placement.
whyWrong.D: Talks only about Vaganova and first position, so no comparison of any kind is made.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that mentions both positions without checking whether it links them as alike or as different.

whyCorrect: The second sentence is the definition of the blank: scholars "inadvertently overlook nuances" when they focus on the obvious transcendentalist features. The blank needs a word meaning to treat subtleties as unimportant or to disregard them, and "discount" is exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "Magnify" means to make subtleties more prominent, the reverse of overlooking them.
whyWrong.B: "Scrutinize" means to examine closely, which is what the scholars fail to do with the nuances.
whyWrong.D: "Denounce" means to condemn publicly, an attack on the subtleties rather than a failure to notice them.

tips: When the next sentence starts with "for instance," it is usually restating the blank in plainer words — read it first.

whyCorrect: The phrase after the dash explains the blank: she is "drawing from memories of her childhood" and "details of her current surroundings." Drawing on lived experience to make art is being inspired by it, and the sentence's structure — no matter what she creates, this is always her source — points to a positive, sourcing relationship.

whyWrong.A: "Complimented by" means praised by someone; direct experience does not pay compliments, and praise is not what the memories provide.
whyWrong.B: "Uncertain about" contradicts the rest of the sentence, which shows her drawing confidently on specific memories and surroundings.
whyWrong.C: "Unbothered by" would mean experience does not affect her, but the sentence says it is the thing she works from.

commonMistakes: Confusing "complimented" (praised) with "complemented" (completed); even the latter would not fit the idea of drawing material from memory.

whyCorrect: The second sentence says Demosthenes repeatedly argued in public addresses that parrhesia was the very foundation of Athenian democracy — that is, he publicly argued for its value. Someone who publicly advocates an idea is a proponent of it.

whyWrong.B: "A steward" manages or safeguards something entrusted to him; the text shows him arguing for an idea, not administering it.
whyWrong.C: "An apprentice" is a beginner learning a trade under a master, which does not describe a prominent orator championing a principle.
whyWrong.D: "A harbinger" is a sign that something is coming, but parrhesia was already practiced in Athens and Demosthenes was defending it, not foreshadowing it.

tips: Match the blank to the evidence verb — here "characterizing... as the foundation of democracy" in "public addresses" is advocacy.

whyCorrect: "Good" here modifies "height," a measurement, not a person's character. The clause that follows — his height could be judged "even from the seated figure" — tells you he is notably tall, so "good" means large in amount. "Considerable" is the sense of "good" used in phrases like "a good distance" or "a good while."

whyWrong.A: "Well-behaved" describes conduct, and a height cannot behave.
whyWrong.C: "Capable" describes a person's ability; it cannot modify a measurement.
whyWrong.D: "Reliable" would mean the height can be counted on, which makes no sense as a description of stature.

tips: Check what the word actually modifies before choosing a meaning — a common sense of the word applied to the wrong noun is the usual trap.

whyCorrect: The colon means the second half of the sentence restates the hypothesis: the more work people believe went into a piece, the more they appreciate it. That is a statement that effort raises a work's worth in their eyes, so the blank needs a verb meaning to prize or place worth on. "Value" is that verb.

whyWrong.B: "Perform" would mean the viewers themselves do the labor, but the effort described belongs to the artist.
whyWrong.C: "Prevent" makes viewers stop the effort from happening, which has nothing to do with how much they appreciate the result.
whyWrong.D: "Neglect" means to disregard the effort, the opposite of appreciating a piece more when more work went into it.

tips: A colon promises a restatement — read the clause after it and put its idea into one verb before looking at the choices.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: contemporary elements show up in modern A Midsummer Night's Dream productions, and they get there unintentionally. Only this quotation has a designer who was actively trying for period accuracy and only later recognized the 1980s fashion that had crept into the designs — deliberate effort at accuracy plus unnoticed contemporary influence is exactly the unintentional case.

whyWrong.A: Describes attention to period-appropriate accessories with no contemporary element and no mention of the play in question.
whyWrong.B: Names the play but describes flexibility that is chosen on purpose to communicate an idea, which makes the anachronism intentional, not accidental.
whyWrong.C: Argues that costumes should always match the period and criticizes period mixing; it prescribes a standard rather than reporting an unintentional lapse.

commonMistakes: Selecting the choice that merely mentions A Midsummer Night's Dream; the play title alone does not address the "unintentionally" half of the claim.

whyCorrect: The claim is specific: the speaker urges John to look for a relationship with someone else instead of waiting on her. This stanza names other women who might have him, tells him to ask them, and explicitly says not to stay single on her account — both halves of the claim in four lines.

whyWrong.A: Denies that she ever loved him and complains about being pestered, but points him toward no one else.
whyWrong.C: Offers friendship in place of love; it refuses him without suggesting he pursue another relationship.
whyWrong.D: Proposes that they be friends and drop hidden hopes, which again is about their own relationship, not about John seeking someone new.

tips: When the claim has two elements, keep both in mind — several choices will satisfy one of them.

whyCorrect: The claim is that Helena works to reduce the friction between Vanya and the professor. This quotation has her speaking directly to Vanya about the damage done by hate and spiteful tattling and telling him it is his duty to make peace with Serebrakoff — an explicit attempt to defuse the conflict.

whyWrong.A: Shows Helena complaining about her own exhaustion with the professor, which reveals her feelings rather than any peacemaking.
whyWrong.B: Pushes back against how others pity her; she is defending her marriage, not smoothing things between the two men.
whyWrong.D: Is spoken to Sonia about Helena's own unhappiness and never touches the Vanya-professor conflict.

commonMistakes: Picking any quotation in which Helena mentions her husband; the claim requires her to be acting on the conflict, not describing her own state.

whyCorrect: Chain the two studies together. Tarabieh: as perceived environmental risk goes up, likelihood of buying goes down — so lower perceived risk means higher likelihood of buying. The Vietnam study found parents of small children perceived the lowest environmental risk in the skin-care product of any group. Applying Tarabieh's relationship, that lowest risk perception should translate into the highest purchase likelihood, so those parents are the group most likely to buy it.

whyWrong.A: Introduces priorities that neither study measured; the finding is about how much risk parents perceived, not about what they weigh against sustainability.
whyWrong.B: Claims the groups are alike, but the second study explicitly reports parents of small children as the extreme low end of risk perception.
whyWrong.C: Reverses the direction — lower perceived risk predicts more appeal, not less — and compares the product with rival products the studies never examined.

tips: Write the first study as a direction (more risk perceived, less buying), then plug the second study's group into it before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: Desai's cross-country result says that strong democracy paired with low inequality restrains inflation. Austria has exactly that pairing, yet its 2017 inflation was higher than Cameroon's. If Austria's political structure should have pushed its inflation down and it was still the higher of the two, then that structure cannot be what produced the gap — something else about 2017 must account for it.

whyWrong.B: Credits inequality differences with most of the gap, but under Desai's finding Austria's low inequality should have lowered its inflation, not raised it above Cameroon's.
whyWrong.C: Questions the indices' accuracy, which nothing in the text does; Desai's study takes measured democratic strength as given and changes the interpretation, not the measurement.
whyWrong.D: Endorses the very critique Desai's result undercuts — that diluted state control drives inflation up — and it also speculates about a scenario the study never tested.

commonMistakes: Reading the Austria-Cameroon pair as evidence for the critique and then choosing an option that agrees with it; the sentence's "but" signals that Desai's finding overrides that first impression.

whyCorrect: "Olga Shurchkov of Wellesley College studies worker productivity" and "other researchers investigate areas such as market behavior and consumer behavior" are both complete sentences, so they need a semicolon between them, not a comma. "For instance" belongs to the first clause — Shurchkov is the example of the "variety of topics" — and as an interrupter at the end of that clause it takes a comma before it.

whyWrong.A: Places the semicolon correctly but drops the comma that must set off "for instance" from "productivity."
whyWrong.C: Attaches "for instance" to the second clause, which would present "other researchers investigate market behavior" as an example of Shurchkov studying productivity — it is a separate case, not an instance of it.
whyWrong.D: Uses commas on both sides, so two independent clauses end up joined by a comma: a comma splice.

tips: Decide which clause the interrupter modifies before you decide where the semicolon goes; both questions have to be answered together.

whyCorrect: "He did not play drums on the label's classic song 'Rapper's Delight'" and "he joined the label after the song's release" are both complete sentences, so a comma alone cannot join them. "However" belongs to the first clause: it contrasts with the previous sentence, which says Chambers is best known as Sugar Hill's house drummer. Ending that clause with ", however" and then using a semicolon links the statement to the explanation that follows.

whyWrong.A: Leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma; "however" is an adverb and cannot do a conjunction's work.
whyWrong.C: Punctuates correctly but moves "However" onto the second clause, making joining the label a contrast with not playing on the song — the second clause is the reason for the first, not a reversal of it.
whyWrong.D: Gives no punctuation at all between the two clauses and no comma around "however," producing a run-on.

commonMistakes: Assuming "however" always opens the second sentence; it just as often closes the first, and here the contrast points backward.

whyCorrect: Look at the end of the text: "2008 FC76, showing no such activity, is considered dormant" is the main clause, and "the object 2060 Chiron is considered an active centaur, showing sporadic comet-like activity" is a second complete clause sitting right before it with only a comma between them. Adding "while" turns the Chiron clause into a subordinate clause, which fixes that splice, and the colon lets the complete sentence ending in "behavior" introduce the two-part explanation of what those differences are.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon after "behavior" is legal, but with no "while" the Chiron clause and the FC76 clause remain two sentences joined by a comma.
whyWrong.B: Same problem as A — the period fixes one boundary and leaves the comma splice between the two centaur descriptions untouched.
whyWrong.D: Adds "while" but only a comma after "behavior," so "they exhibit striking differences in behavior, while the object 2060 Chiron is considered an active centaur" reads as a finished sentence and the FC76 clause is spliced on.

tips: Count the independent clauses in the whole sentence, not just around the blank — this one has a second boundary problem further along.

whyCorrect: "Compiled" is the verb and "climate data from several sites in Puerto Rico's Luquillo Mountains" is its direct object. Nothing may come between a verb and its object, so the blank takes no punctuation at all.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, and "climate data from several sites..." is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete sentence, but "researchers... compiled" breaks off before the verb has an object.
whyWrong.D: A comma here separates the verb from the object it acts on, which Standard English does not allow.

commonMistakes: Reading the long list of names as a signal that punctuation is needed; the names are the subject and the sentence still runs straight into its verb and object.

whyCorrect: "Okinaka doesn't make such decisions single-handedly" and "all historical designations must be approved by a group of nine other experts" are both complete sentences. "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join them — it can only sit inside one of them. Ending the first sentence with "single-handedly, however." and starting a new sentence with "All" is the only option that gives each clause its own sentence.

whyWrong.A: Produces the classic comma splice: two independent clauses with only "however" and commas between them.
whyWrong.B: "and" needs a comma before it to join two independent clauses, and "however and" stacks two connectives that do opposite jobs.
whyWrong.C: Runs the two sentences together with no punctuation and leaves "however" unmarked.

tips: Treat "however," "therefore," and "moreover" as adverbs that cannot glue two sentences together no matter how many commas surround them.

whyCorrect: The sentence has a subject — "emulsifiers such as stearyl alcohol" — but no main verb until the blank supplies one. "Are employed" is a finite verb in the passive voice, plural to match "emulsifiers," and it lets the infinitive "to blend oil and water" state the purpose.

whyWrong.A: "Employed" alone is a past participle here with no helping verb, so the sentence is left without a working main verb.
whyWrong.B: "Being employed" is a participle phrase, not a finite verb; the sentence never reaches a predicate.
whyWrong.D: "That they employ" starts a relative clause and reverses the roles, making the emulsifiers the ones doing the employing, and it still leaves the sentence without a main verb.

tips: Find the subject, then ask whether the sentence ever gets a verb that could carry tense; an -ing or bare -ed form cannot.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank says Montaigne constantly questions his own perspective. The sentence after gives his motto, "What do I know?" — a question that does exactly that. The motto suits the habit, so the transition needs to signal appropriateness, which is what "Fittingly" does.

whyWrong.A: "Still" concedes a point despite something previously said, but the motto reinforces the previous sentence rather than pushing against it.
whyWrong.B: "Conversely" announces an opposite, and a self-questioning motto is not the opposite of a habit of self-questioning.
whyWrong.D: "Nowadays" contrasts the present with the past, but both sentences describe Montaigne in his own time.

tips: When the second sentence is an illustration that matches the first perfectly, look for a word meaning "appropriately" before considering contrast words.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank states Brown's general claim — ornaments can serve a purpose. The sentence after names one such purpose: communicating information about a city's history and culture. That is a specific case of the general claim, so the transition must introduce an example.

whyWrong.A: "However" sets up a contrast, but the second sentence supports Brown's claim instead of qualifying it.
whyWrong.B: "As a result" makes the communicating a consequence of Brown's argument; it is an instance of what she argued, not an effect of her arguing it.
whyWrong.D: "Finally" closes a list, and no earlier purposes have been given for this one to conclude.

commonMistakes: Choosing "However" because the passage contains a disagreement between Loos and Brown; that contrast happens one sentence earlier, not at the blank.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes a place — India. The second gives a production figure but never names where it applies, so the transition has to supply that link. "There" means "in India," attaching the 18.8 million metric tons to the country just named.

whyWrong.A: "Hence" claims the production figure follows logically from one mango variety originating in India, which it does not.
whyWrong.C: "In fact" intensifies or confirms the previous statement, but the production total does not confirm where the Cheruku rasamu comes from.
whyWrong.D: "Specifically" narrows a general statement to a precise case, yet the second sentence is about total national output, not a narrower detail about that one variety.

tips: When the second sentence is missing a place or time that the first sentence supplies, the transition is doing locating work, not logical work.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: give an example of a film Prieto worked on. That means the sentence has to name Prieto and name a film. Only this choice does both, identifying Frida (2002) as a film he shot.

whyWrong.A: Names Prieto and a director but never names a film, so no example of a film is given.
whyWrong.C: Describes filmmaking in general and mentions neither Prieto nor any film.
whyWrong.D: Explains what a cinematographer does; it names Prieto but no particular film.

tips: When the goal says "provide an example of X," the sentence must actually contain an X — here, a film title.

whyCorrect: An objective is what the study set out to do. The notes state it directly: a primary aim was to determine the benefits of UNAs in these cities. This choice reports that aim as the point of the sentence, which is what "emphasize an objective" asks for.

whyWrong.A: Gives the study's duration and location — facts about how it was run, not what it was trying to find out.
whyWrong.B: Mentions an objective only in a subordinate opener and then makes the sentence about what was examined, so the emphasis lands on the forty-four types of UNAs.
whyWrong.D: Reports a benefit of large urban parks, which is a finding about the subject matter rather than a goal of the study.

commonMistakes: Accepting a sentence that merely contains the word "objective"; check what the main clause is actually about.

whyCorrect: The notes are about a 2019 Oahu study of seed dispersal, and the sentence that best represents the study presents both what the researchers did — catalogued seeds in bird fecal samples — and why they did it: to learn what role non-native birds play in dispersing seeds. The other choices report isolated details about individual plant species instead of the study itself.

whyWrong.A: States a background fact about Oahu's plants and reduces the study to nothing; it also treats one catalogued species as evidence for "most" species.
whyWrong.B: Compares the native status of two plants, a detail from the notes that says nothing about the study's work or purpose.
whyWrong.D: Lists two species found in the samples but omits the reason the researchers were looking, so the study's aim disappears.

commonMistakes: This item's goal sentence does not match its notes — it asks about the order in which supercontinents formed, which nothing in the notes concerns — so judge the choices by which one best represents the 2019 seed-dispersal study.
